rejection_findings.finding: obs_protagoras_0006 supports the 310d legal framing, laughter, and money-for-wisdom remedy, but the rewrite also makes checkable claims about naming the sophist's object and entrusting the soul across 313a-313c without citing an accepted record for those moves.

obs_protagoras_0079, obs_protagoras_0248, and obs_protagoras_0084 support the myth through 322c. The rewrite's added 322d claim about universal distribution and only a few being unable to make a city lacks matching accepted evidence.

claim_protagoras_0034, claim_protagoras_0035, and claim_protagoras_0036 support the 343c-344b reading of Simonides as refuting Pittacus and shifting from being good to becoming good. They do not support the added 344c claim about remaining good or the exact 347a Hippias handoff.

revisions.title: When eagerness is treated as a grievance
revisions.body: At the opening, Socrates treats Hippocrates’ agitation about Protagoras as if it might be a grievance. Hippocrates laughs and answers that Protagoras is wise but does not make him wise. Socrates then recasts the excitement as a transaction: give Protagoras money, persuade him, and he will make you wise. The laughter keeps that remedy unstable, inviting us to hear the buyer’s urgency as something to examine.

revisions.title: Technical wisdom is not civic wisdom
revisions.body: The myth’s crucial contrast is between technical and political provision. Epimetheus distributes bodily powers by compensating among mortal kinds. Prometheus gives humans technical wisdom with fire, but political wisdom remains with Zeus. Zeus then sends Hermes with respect and right because, without those qualities, humans wrong one another and scatter. Civic order appears here as a distinct gift, not as a consequence of technical skill alone.

revisions.title: A poem read against Pittacus
revisions.body: Socrates reads Simonides’ poem as a refutation of Pittacus. The hinge is a shift from being good to becoming good: becoming a good person is hard. He reinforces this by treating “truly” as a question of word order, then states that the poem’s chief work is to refute Pittacus. Hear the result as Socrates’ reconstruction, not a neutral report.
